children: The Prime Minister asks Indian businesses to strengthen domestic production, improve product standards and use new trade agreements to expand their presence in overseas markets

Prime Minister Narendra Modi has called on Indian industry to reduce its reliance on imports in sectors such as pharmaceuticals and metals, arguing that domestic manufacturers need to build stronger production capabilities rather than depend on overseas suppliers. He also criticised businesses for treating India's large consumer market as a source of assured demand instead of improving product quality and international competitiveness.

Addressing the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (Ficci)'s annual general meeting on Thursday, Modi said companies needed to make greater investments in domestic manufacturing and prepare for changing requirements in international markets. He urged industry leaders to use the opportunities created by India's recently signed free trade agreements (FTAs) to expand exports, develop market-specific products and establish distribution networks overseas.

The Prime Minister said the size of India's domestic market should not discourage companies from pursuing international growth. He also questioned the industry's approach to product standards, arguing that Indian consumers should not receive products of a different quality from those manufactured for export markets.

Modi's concerns extended to employment and compensation practices. Referring to the reduction in the corporate tax rate from 30 per cent to 22 per cent in 2019, he questioned whether businesses had used the resulting tax benefits to increase salaries or expand their workforce. He also referred to the increase in the income tax exemption threshold to Rs 12 lakh in 2025, asking companies to demonstrate a greater contribution to employment generation.

The remarks prompted a response from Mohandas Pai, investor and former chief financial officer (CFO) of Infosys, who criticised the difference between compensation for senior management and starting salaries for employees.

“Thanks PM Narendra Modi, for asking these questions of India Inc. They have massively hiked CEO compensation and board compensation in many cases but starting salaries in many cases for the last 10 years are barely above inflation. These cos should be exposed for hurting young Indians,” Pai wrote on X.

Modi also asked Indian businesses to develop concrete plans to benefit from the country's recently concluded trade agreements with major economies. He said improved access to international markets would create opportunities for domestic manufacturers, but companies would need to invest in understanding overseas consumers and meeting their requirements.

He emphasised that long-term investment decisions should account for India's strategic and economic interests, particularly as access to resources and supply chains becomes increasingly important in international trade. Building domestic capabilities, he said, would strengthen self-reliance while creating additional opportunities for businesses.

Agriculture and food processing were among the sectors identified for greater private investment. Modi pointed to India's estimated 2-2.5 per cent share of global agricultural exports and called for companies to increase their participation in processing, manufacturing and value addition.

He cited an increase in the share of processed food in India's agri-food exports from 13 per cent to more than 20 per cent over the past 12 years. Greater investment in processing infrastructure, he indicated, could help Indian businesses move further up the value chain and capture a larger share of international demand.
The Prime Minister also identified hand tools, power tools and machinery as manufacturing categories with export potential, particularly in developing economies and countries across the Global South.

Modi questioned the continued distinction made by manufacturers between products intended for domestic consumption and those supplied to overseas markets. He argued that Indian companies needed to apply consistent quality standards across both markets rather than position superior specifications as an export-only offering.

He also urged businesses to study consumer preferences in individual international markets before expanding their product portfolios. Investments in meeting foreign quality requirements, adapting products and establishing distribution networks would be necessary to build a sustainable export presence, he said.

On the government's reform agenda, Modi invited industry representatives to communicate their concerns and recommendations directly, including suggestions on areas where policy changes were needed. Describing the administration as a business-friendly government, he said feedback from companies would help identify shortcomings and inform further reforms.

The address placed the onus on Indian industry to complement government initiatives with investments in domestic production, employment, product quality and export infrastructure. Reducing import dependence, meanwhile, remains central to the broader push for stronger domestic manufacturing capabilities.
